a7719ef45c037686: After being defeated in the elections, the senator fled to the US with his family
Originally published on Global Voices
Art by Global Voices with Canva Pro. Photo by the Brazilian Senate. Fair use.

Forty-eight hours after losing the runoff in Brazil to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Flávio Bolsonaro, former president Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son, a senator representing Rio de Janeiro, fled to the United States. From there, where his brother Eduardo, a former congressman, has lived since February 2025, he continues to challenge the results of the election he lost by 4.4 million votes, as attested by the Electoral Court (TSE), the Organization of American States (OAS), and other right-led governments in the region.

Upon landing in Miami, Flávio published a letter proclaiming himself “the true president of Brazil” and “president-elect of Brazil.” After 22 minutes — and a demand from the US Department of State — he retracted to “the leader of Brazil.”

US President Donald Trump had said that Brazil’s elections “looked rigged,” but he wouldn't “get involved.” The New York Times reported, however, that Flávio was helped by Trump's aides. “The jet [he traveled on] had been arranged by a White House official,” affirmed the newspaper.

Flávio’s narrative is that he is being persecuted by the Brazilian justice system and Lula’s government as an opposition leader, since the Supreme Court ordered the seizure of his passports — he also has Italian citizenship — right after his defeat was announced.

Justice Alexandre de Moraes, considered a foe of the Bolsonaro family and himself under suspicion for having links to the same disgraced banker connected to Flávio, issued the order in response to a Federal Police request that considered Flávio a flight risk. In Brazil, a president cannot be investigated for alleged crimes committed before their term, meaning that once elected, all pending investigations involving Flávio would have been suspended. This is also the first time in 24 years that Flávio will not have a seat to ensure his parliamentary immunity.

According to the Brazilian Federal Police, three elements indicated a flight risk in Flávio’s case: an interview his brother Eduardo gave to a podcast in the US defending the idea of him leaving the country, on October 23, his considerable economic power, and well-established structures abroad that could support him in a long stay.

The day after the election, after visiting his father, who is under house arrest convicted for a coup attempt, Flávio recorded a video complaining about the measure, claiming “he never thought about leaving the country” and promising to stay and answer to investigations. Overnight, apparently, he had a change of heart in time for a new plan.

Investigations and corruption suspicions have long surrounded his name. In 2020, Sergio Moro, the judge who convicted Lula, resigned as Bolsonaro’s justice minister, accusing the president of trying to intervene with the Federal Police to protect Flávio in an embezzlement and money-laundering inquiry. In a cabinet meeting, then-president Bolsonaro shouted at his ministers: “I won’t wait until they fuck my entire family,” saying he would fire whoever got in their way.

During this election campaign, skeletons in Flávio's closet were further exposed in stories published by the Brazilian press. Global Voices gathered the main ones here. Flávio is currently under three investigations at the Supreme Court.
Rachadinha

This is the case that led Jair Bolsonaro to allegedly interfere in the Federal Police in 2020. Flávio was indicted by Rio’s Public Prosecution Office for embezzlement, money laundering, and criminal organization. The case was later adjourned. Rachadinha (“split” in English) is a salary kickback scheme in which a politician hires someone for a certain position and then reclaims part of their salary.

In 2018, after Bolsonaro’s election, a report by the Council for Financial Activities Control (Coaf) pointed to atypical financial movements in the account of Flávio’s aide, Fabricio Queiroz, an old friend of his father. Queiroz, who was filmed paying for Flávio's daughters’ tuition in cash, was identified as the scheme’s operator. For the Public Prosecution Office, according to UOL news outlet, the scheme was used to cover Flávio’s personal expenses and to increase his patrimony.

There were also suspicions that a chocolate franchise shop, owned by Flávio, was used for money laundering. The investigation found 1,512 cash deposits in repeated amounts between March 2015 and December 2018 at the establishment.

An audio recording found by police in 2024 shows then-president Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio’s attorneys, and Alexandre Ramagem, former director of the Brazilian Intelligence Agency (Abin), currently a fugitive living in the US, allegedly discussing a plan to free Flávio from the investigations through Federal Revenue Service employees.
‘Dark Horse’ and Vorcaro

On May 13, 2026, The Intercept Brasil published a story and an audio recording showing that the movie “Dark Horse,” a biopic about Jair Bolsonaro, starring Jim Caviezel, could have been financed by disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro. Before the story went out, a reporter from the news outlet asked Flávio about the case. The senator laughed and dismissed the question, saying: “That’s a lie! Where did you get this from?”

Vorcaro is at the center of one of the country's biggest scandals, involving politicians, members of the Supreme Court and other judges, and celebrities, through his bank, Master — its license was approved during Jair Bolsonaro’s government. Vorcaro is investigated for a fraud scheme that caused a BRL 47 billion (around USD 8.7 billion) loss to the Credit Guarantee Fund (FGC), which backs Brazil's banking system.

The messages published by The Intercept show Flávio negotiating with Vorcaro on WhatsApp. Flávio asked for BRL 134 million (USD 24.9 million) and received at least BRL 61 million (USD 11.17 million). In one of the last messages between them, before Vorcaro was arrested while trying to flee the country, Flávio tells him: “Brother, I am and will always be with you; there is no half-talk between us,” reported TIB.
Since he couldn’t deny their link, Flávio has repeated that the money he negotiated with Vorcaro was “private money for a private movie.”

This is also one of the investigations into Flávio at the Federal Supreme Court (STF), which targets the movie’s financing operation. Despite the movie being filmed in Brazil, Vorcaro sent the money to a fund in the US (Havengate), managed by a friend of Eduardo Bolsonaro’s. The final destination for the money hasn't been confirmed yet.
Willer Thomaz, a friend

Another inquiry investigates Flávio for money laundering and currency evasion, along with his friend Willer Tomaz, a Brazilian lawyer also currently in the US. Tomaz is under investigation for money laundering through betting companies and involvement in another scandal, a fraud scheme at the national pension fund (INSS).
Documents accessed by Brazilian news outlets showed that Tomaz alone moved BRL 5 billion (around USD 930 million) in betting sites and cashed out BRL 200 million (USD 37.2 million).

When Piauí magazine revealed that Flávio had travelled in Vorcaro’s plane with his family, the senator’s first reaction was to say that “fortunately, it was Willer's.” His friend shared the plane’s quotas with a Vorcaro company. Tomaz denied ever meeting with the banker.

In October, O Globo newspaper published that Flávio had been registered as a “master user” on an offshore account under the name of a company managed by Tomaz and registered on Madeira Island, Portugal. This status could give him “significant operational access,” according to the Federal Police. Piauí magazine also says the senator could have been an indirect partner in a betting company based in São Paulo, but controlled by another company registered in Madeira, also linked to Tomaz. Flávio denies it.

Folha de S. Paulo newspaper says that the relationship between Flávio and Tomaz began in 2019. During the COVID-19 parliamentary inquiry commission at the National Congress, two years later, the senator defended Tomaz, calling him a friend. They always denied being business associates, claiming they were only friends.
Ana Clara’s death and the militias

On the morning of February 2, 2021, five-year-old Ana Clara Machado was shot and killed while playing at the doorstep of her home, in Rio de Janeiro. The Military Police denied any confrontation or the presence of narcos in the area where their operation was taking place. Later, the Civil Police identified police officer Bruno Delaroli as the shooter and arrested him. In March, 2026, ICL Notícias, a news website, reported that Flávio Bolsonaro worked on the officer's defense team in the higher courts, trying to avoid a jury trial. Another news outlet, UOL, revealed he worked pro bono. Lula questioned the senator about his motives during a debate on TV Globo.
Also, according to ICL, this wasn’t the only case Flávio advocated for officers accused of killings. Folha says his career as a defense lawyer gained traction after he was elected senator.

During his political life, Flávio has had a long history of links to police officers identified as members of so-called militias — paramilitary groups mostly formed by active and retired officers, carrying out vigilante and organized crime activities in dominated territories. When a state deputy in Rio, Flávio employed at his office the mother and wife of Adriano da Nobrega, an ex-military policeman, linked to a militia known as Crime Office, whose main activities were to execute ordered killings. He also sent parliamentary money to an NGO connected to another police officer involved in the murder of Rio’s city councillor Marielle Franco. According to Piauí magazine, the militia man known as “Peixe” (fish) referred to Flávio as “our senator.”
ICL News says the UN will examine Flávio's links to the militias when analyzing Ana Clara’s case.
Written by Global Voices Brazil
74ed475c846c9cfc: I’ve been locked in to my various screens since results from midterm elections started to roll in last night. And it didn’t take long to see the beginning of the blue wave: Democrats took control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, a dramatic swing from Donald Trump’s victory two years ago.

While the results are striking, we probably won’t be seeing some of the big climate and energy policy shifts that have come in recent years as Congress and the presidency have changed hands. Instead, we’re entering a period of divided government, with a Congress that will likely do battle with Trump’s White House over the next two years. But even if the federal government isn’t likely to pass laws that overhaul energy and climate policy, the midterm results could be a big deal for energy, especially at the state and local level.

Let’s step back for just a moment to put these results in context. Readers might remember huge laws affecting climate and energy that were passed in just the last four years. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act included massive support for clean energy, including tax credits and government grants and loans. Then the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act essentially slashed much of the support and financial incentives in the IRA from two years before.

What those two laws had in common was a period when the government was entirely united, with the Senate, House of Representatives, and presidency all controlled by the same party—the Democrats in the first case and the Republicans in the second.

Now Democrats have captured a majority in both the Senate and the House. But Donald Trump is still in the White House. And crucially, neither chamber is anywhere close to a two-thirds Democratic majority. That’s the ratio that would be needed to override a presidential veto.

So even if Congress puts together new legislation to boost climate measures and clean energy, Trump will need to sign it—and that dramatically narrows the scope of what might happen legislatively between now and the next election.

There could be some bipartisan compromises. One interesting bit of legislation to watch immediately after the election is what happens with permitting reform. In late September, a bipartisan group of senators put forward a bill that would overhaul how new energy projects are reviewed and approved in the US. The law aims to cut red tape and speed up the permitting process.

The Senate is set to vote on that package, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, on November 9, before the new Congress takes control in January. The White House has supported the bill, and it could pass the Senate if just a handful of Democrats join the Republican majority. But now, we might see Democrats wait until next year to try to renegotiate a deal, though anything would still need to pass muster with Trump.

With Democratic control of Congress, we’ll likely see much more scrutiny of Trump and agencies controlled by his appointees. Democratic leaders have already signaled plans to go after leaders like EPA commissioner Lee Zeldin over cuts to staff and investments. Democrats will have the power to subpoena cabinet members and open investigations.

Looking beyond the national results, a major trend to watch moving forward will be local action. Democrats swept local control of Pennsylvania, and officials there have signaled plans to support renewable energy and efforts to cut greenhouse-gas emissions. Democrats also took control of the Georgia Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years. The group regulates electric utilities, essentially controlling much of the grid’s buildout.

Among the broadest effects of these election results, though, will be for the data center industry. According to tracking from Ballotpedia, there were 41 local ballot questions related to data centers. And overwhelmingly, voters chose to restrict their development. Nearly every single one of these measures looks set to come down against data center development, as of the morning of November 4.

And AI critics fared well in their races, too. Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governor’s seat in Texas, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. During her campaign, Hinojosa called for a law to completely pause data center development; if passed, it could have major implications for both the state’s grid and the data center industry more broadly.

We might not see dramatic new climate- or energy-related federal legislation between now and the next major US election. But many voters signaled, and quite loudly, that they wanted a change. We’ll see how much will shift in the next two years, and where that leaves us.

1ff2567b9abdb34e: 250 House seats, ~55 Senate seats.
The past few months have been fascinating, watching pundits wrestle with what would become a historic election.

All presidents lose Congressional seats in the midterms (with only 4 exceptions). Given how close the margins had been, a shift in at least the House was likely. But this particular president has been uniquely polarizing. He won in 2024 by broadening traditional Republican demographics, adding a coalition that included young males, the uneducated, and Hispanics. That left the GOP coalition vulnerable in a normal midterm. How did that it turn out?
Everywhere I looked – stock futures, prediction markets, polls – turned out to be a panoply of errors.

Stock futures were in a deep selloff by 6 p.m.; prediction markets underpriced Democratic candidates; and the Polls, which got the general direction of the race right, had significant errors in the magnitude of the changes and wildly misread Democratic wins in traditionally GOP strongholds.
The S&P sold off about 100 points; now it’s up 150 points from those lows. At ~noon today we are +3% on the Dow and +2% on the SPX and NDX; that’s quite a swing.
maybe double-check your math…?
About those Prediction Markets:
The FT reported that “Polymarket’s gamblers had a bad night of forecasting, undermining the reputation of prediction markets.” (I have been criticizing their inaccuracy forever).
And the Polls!

The margins were far wider than even the final polls suggested; polling missed the “Texas Shock” where Talarico won a Senate seat by ~10 points and over a million votes; Gina Hinojosa won the Texas Governor’s race by 7% and 750k votes; traditional red states like Kansas and South Carolina elected Democratic senators for the first time in nearly a century. The so-called “Shy Trump” voter vanished; exit polls said 43% of voters cast ballots to oppose Trump vs 16% who supported him. Turnout Models missed intense motivation among Dem-leaning voters.

Some right-wing politicians imagined the MAGA coalition would last, but it showed signs of fraying almost immediately after the 2024 election. Each of the president’s three signature policies was a factor in the coalition pieces I mentioned to start: 1) ICE‘s aggressive immigration enforcement; 2) War, and a muscular foreign policy supporting multiple wars; 3) Inflation, driven partly by a silly tariff policy.

Whenever I channel William Goldman to emphasize how little we know about the future, I feel I am cheating, taking advantage of a flaw in the human condition that most either don’t know or don’t care about. We evolved in a very specific environment to deal with threats very different from the ones we face today.

Tribalism, a bad information diet, and an inability to accurately assess our own skill sets are a poor tool set when analyzing social events and politics. It is an utterly fatal combination when putting capital to work in markets…

Each time someone takes a photo of their meal at a participating restaurant and shares it on social media, GiftAMeal donates to a local food bank. We ran two versions of GiftAMeal’s Facebook ad, which together reached 67,576 people. One said the company “donated 25,000 meals every month” last year. The other said it “donated 300,000 meals” last year. Both were true, and everything else about the ads was the same. We found that people who saw the monthly version were about 21% more likely to click on the ad. Next, we worked with Salt + Smoke, a Midwestern barbecue restaurant. When we emailed 75,514 customers who subscribed to its newsletters, half read that the company would give $5,000 a month from September through December to a small, local charity that supports early childhood education programs. The other half read that it would make a one-time donation of $20,000. Subscribers who read about the monthly donation pledge were nearly twice as likely to click through to the restaurant’s website as those who read about the one-time gift pledge even though the total was the same. Then we ran online experiments with more than 7,400 people to learn why and when consistent giving makes people view a company more favorably. We found that, on average, when a company gives monthly, people see its charitable support as a more genuine commitment to the causes. Why it matters U.S. companies gave nearly $44 billion in 2025 alone. And this kind of giving is popular with the public. In a 2022 survey, 88% of Americans said it’s important for companies to make the world a better place. Companies frequently promote their donations with the largest numbers they can muster. For example, Microsoft announced that the software giant and its employees donated $256 million in 2025; Walmart and its foundation say they have donated $2 billion in 2026. Yet boasting about big numbers may not impress people as much as emphasizing the consistency of donations. This may help explain why companies often struggle to convey their charitable efforts in ways that win people over. Even if companies give only once a year, they can indicate that they are engaged in a steady pattern of giving. For example, they can make their annual gifts on Giving Tuesday every year. Donating on the same day or as part of the same fundraising campaign every year can signal an ongoing commitment, not a one-off. What still isn’t known We don’t yet know how long the reputational boost companies may get from recurring donations might last, or whether those donations can translate into long-term customer loyalty. It’s also possible that what we found would not apply during emergencies. For example, consumers might be happy to see a company make one big gift right after a hurricane when a local community’s needs are immense. What’s next Along with Park and Cynthia Cryder, a Washington University in St. Louis marketing professor, I’m now studying other ways that corporate philanthropy can affect how much credit companies get for doing good. So far, we’ve found that companies may earn less goodwill when they ask customers to chip in to their charitable campaigns. People seem to expect companies to carry more of the load themselves. The Research Brief is a short take about interesting academic work. 416b7eba9f32ddf4: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents.

This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem.

Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows.

d3140bfa455d8dce: No justice for Bangladeshi workers who are recruited into Russia’s war
Originally published on Global Voices
War-wounded Bangladeshis in Russia plead to return home. Screenshot from a YouTube report by Ekhon TV. Fair use.

Maksudur Rahman was 31 when a labor recruiter arrived in his hometown in Lakshmipur district, southeastern Bangladesh, with a job offer: becoming a janitor in Russia. Nearly every family in the district has someone working overseas, so the pitch landed. According to an international investigation, he borrowed money and paid the broker BDT 1.2 million (about USD 9,800). For a household like his, that is a fortune, but the promised wages made the debt look manageable. He signed up and flew out.

What followed had nothing to do with brooms. Within weeks, he was on the front lines of Russia’s war in Ukraine. He and three other Bangladeshi workers were handed a paper written in Russian — a language they did not understand — and told to sign. Then came an army camp, where recruits were trained in drone tactics, medical evacuation, and heavy weapons. When Rahman protested, a Russian commander replied through a translation app that his own agent had sent him there. Workers in his group were threatened with ten-year jail terms and beaten, he said.

His story is a case study in how this insidious war pipeline operates: a local agent, a borrowed fortune, a contract nobody could read, and a war that was never part of the bargain. But to understand how a man from Lakshmipur ended up in that camp, it’s important to look at the realities in Russia and what is driving these recruitment traps.
A war that is running out of men

Russia has a manpower problem, and the figures are hard to wave away. Enlistment into contract service dropped about 20 percent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to international reporting relayed by Ukrainian outlets. This deficit persists even though Moscow is offering signing packages of up to USD 80,000 and debt write-offs of up to USD 140,000.

Meanwhile, BBC and Mediazona journalists estimate there have been at least 300,000 Russian deaths since the war began on February 24, 2022, based on local obituaries. Other Western intelligence estimates put Russian deaths near 500,000, with monthly casualties of 30,000 to 35,000.

One estimate says the country needs another 1.5 million workers to stabilize its labor market, and officials themselves expect a shortfall of 3.1 million people by 2030. Because stricter migration rules have also pushed out roughly a million temporary workers, the army and the factories now compete for the same shrinking labor pool.

While Russia has not dared to implement another full-scale military draft as it did in September 2022 — a move that was highly damaging to the regime and local support — officials are doing everything they can to buy recruits or force those who are vulnerable, elderly, or simply went to the draft station to register to go to the front lines.
Given these manpower challenges, Moscow has looked outward. It has already used tens of thousands of prisoners and three waves of North Korean troops, yet that wasn’t enough.

A UK defense assessment, summarized by a Ukrainian outlet, says the supply of convict recruits is probably exhausted, and Russia is widening its search across the Global South to avoid another mobilization at home.
Ukrainian data counts nearly 29,000 foreigners who have signed contracts since 2022. One report says the army wants at least 18,500 more in 2026, naming Bangladesh among its top targets.

Rights groups see a pattern behind these numbers. The International Federation for Human Rights described an organized pipeline aimed at undocumented migrants, detainees, precarious workers, and foreign students across three continents, and Amnesty International accused Moscow last month of deceptive, coercive, and exploitative recruitment.
Who is accepting this offer?

Within South Asia, this recruitment scheme goes beyond just Bangladesh. After Sri Lanka’s economic collapse in 2022 and Nepal’s recession, wages of at least USD 550 a month in Russia looked like a way out, according to analysis from the Observer Research Foundation (ORF). Nepal’s foreign minister admitted in early 2024 that more than 200 Nepali citizens had been recruited. Kathmandu later suspended work permits for Russia after numerous Nepali citizens died on the front lines in Ukraine. Sri Lanka, for its part, saw an estimated 600 to 700 former soldiers recruited.

Why, then, would anyone take the risk? Money comes first. One welder, according to a report on survivors’ accounts, was offered a USD 20,990 signing bonus, a salary of USD 2,664 per month, and a shot at citizenship. For families buried in debt, those numbers can drown out the danger.

But money isn’t the whole answer. Some Bangladeshis enlisted knowingly were misled about the role, the reporting noted, while others lost a visa-linked job and found a recruiter waiting with a better-sounding contract. Some never aimed for Russia at all: One prisoner said an Uzbek broker had promised him residence in Italy. Once inside, the choice largely disappears, as recruits were presented with contracts in Russian, with those who hesitated facing threats and violence, according to Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds. Another report described passports and phones seized on arrival.
The legal door and the missing agreement

Russia was never a typical destination for Bangladeshi workers. This labor force first entered the country via shipyards, where skilled hands were needed as the war strained the domestic labor supply. Initially, around 56 workers were sent there. Then the flow increased. According to the data of the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU), 993 Bangladeshis went in 2024 and 4,663 in 2025. The Bureau of Manpower Employment and Training (BMET) records 8,247 departures between 2024 and June 2026. The state-run Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) sent just 426 among them, and those workers are reported safe; the private market carried the rest.

However, even with this sizable flow of workers, no signed labor agreement seems to exist between the two countries. During Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman’s June 2026 visit to Moscow, both sides merely urged early conclusion of pending accords, including a human resource agreement and a readmission agreement. Russia has agreed to fast-track a proposal for 100,000 Bangladeshi workers within a year. A state minister even spoke of 300,000 to 400,000 workers over five years. Meanwhile, Dhaka’s embassy in Moscow has asked Russia to bar Bangladeshis from military service.
The lack of a formal agreement leaves Bangladeshi workers exposed and vulnerable to scams and exploitation.
Fraud also shows up outside the war. In January 2026, 35 workers returned from Russia after being terminated, saying they had each paid about BDT 700,000 (roughly USD 5,651).
Agents, agencies, and the price of a seat

The route from village to barracks runs through ordinary offices. Bangladesh’s Special Response Battalion (SRB) said 30 men who flew to Russia in May 2026 went through three manpower firms, Jabal-e-Noor International, RS International, and TS Group. Officers arrested two alleged ringleaders in mid-October and say a Russian man and a Kyrgyz woman were part of the network, though these allegations remain unconfirmed. The expatriates’ welfare minister told Parliament that the men left with BMET clearance through licensed agencies, which shows that paperwork alone proves nothing.

Once the men landed, the script repeated. Their passports and phones were taken. After 21 days of training, they went to the front. Investigators said they were used as bait to expose enemy positions to drones.
Counting the dead without a count

Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds identified at least 104 Bangladeshis recruited as of February 2026 and at least 34 killed, based on Ukrainian information, and warned that the real toll is probably higher. But on October 14, 2026, the SRB said 20 of the same 30 were dead, with 17 killed by a drone strike on their first day at the front and six still fighting, local news reports said.
These figures can’t simply be added together, because the overlap is unknown and the sources differ: police, rights groups, and Kyiv. Those families, meanwhile, wait without bodies.

Rights groups have urged Dhaka to dismantle the networks and Ukraine to screen captured foreign fighters for signs of trafficking. Yet families still ask for rescue, and the same daily’s editors have pleaded with the government to start bringing the stranded men home.
No Justice for the victims

Back to Maksudur Rahman: He got out, and today he sits at home in Lakshmipur, holding up a Russian military dog tag as proof of where he has been. Others from the same corner of Bangladesh haven’t come home. Sajjad, 20, was killed after being taken to fight, and his father, Mohammed Siraj, now holds a photograph of where his son used to be. For Siraj, justice is not an abstraction. It is a name on a charge sheet, a body to bury, and an answer to the question of who sent his son to war.

In the village, families confronted the recruiting agents and demanded to know why their loved ones were being trained for war. Their questions belong in a courtroom, not only in a village courtyard. Until the agents who sold these jobs and the system that cleared their paperwork are made to answer, the families will keep carrying a debt that is more than money.
Rahman’s loan was real, the war was real, and the janitor’s job never existed. A man who left home to earn a living came back carrying a soldier’s dog tag. And no justice in sight.
Written by Zulker Naeen
914fe66fbaac1cb7: From Moaz Nair
When political parties ride on the back of religion, it is rarely the state that suffers the most – it is the faith itself.

Globally and domestically, the dangerous fusion of the spiritual and the secular has transformed religion from an immutable moral guide into a raw tool for worldly power. When the boundary between the house of worship and the polling booth dissolves, public perception shifts. Faith becomes tethered to the behaviour of opportunistic politicians and the inevitable failures of administration. To protect the sanctity of belief, we must separate religion from partisan politics.
When politicians weaponise faith to mobilise voters, they strip it of its deeper theological and moral complexities.

Religion ceases to be a path towards spiritual growth, universal compassion or ethical governance. Instead, it is flattened into a rigid, polarising political boundary. This exploitation fosters a destructive "us versus them" mentality, making a faith that should champion justice appear intolerant, exclusionary and tribal.
A dangerous paradox

Furthermore, when political parties base their core principles on a specific doctrine, they create a dangerous paradox. If a government aligned with religion becomes corrupt, incompetent or oppressive, the public does not simply blame the politicians – they blame the religion itself. The faith is unseated from its sacred pedestal and recast as a symbol of governance failure.
To prevent this decay, several developed nations have intentionally kept political parties free of religious tags.

Turkey stands as a foundational historical blueprint. Through its secular constitutional framework, it deliberately decoupled state affairs from religious identity to protect both governance and the sanctity of personal faith.

Conversely, where religion and politics aggressively intertwine, modern history offers cautionary tales of profound public disillusionment. In some countries, decades of administrative corruption and economic mismanagement by a clerical state have severely damaged the moral authority of the faith, driving massive waves of domestic secularisation.

In the US, the tight embrace between the Christian Right and partisan factions reduced faith to a few polarising "litmus test" issues, alienating millions of moderate believers and fuelling a rapid rise in the "unchurched" population.

In India, the rise of aggressive majoritarian religious nationalism has systematically reduced vast, ancient philosophical traditions into a rigid checklist for political loyalty, fracturing communities into hostile factions.

These global shifts resonate deeply with current Malaysian political dynamics. For decades, our local landscape has seen a creeping politicisation of faith, where theological monopoly is used as a shortcut to electoral legitimacy. Political actors increasingly reduce the rich ethics of faith to divisive rhetoric and identity policing.
This local trajectory manifests in three highly destructive ways.

First, it forces a reduction of public morality. To win elections, politicians narrow expansive spiritual traditions down to a few polarising, headline-grabbing issues. This allows unqualified figures to dictate what is considered "moral" purely to suit campaign agendas.

We see this tension play out vividly in modern policy gridlocks such as the intense debates over reforming historical university admission quotas. Critical socioeconomic solutions to address specialist medical shortages were immediately hijacked and framed as a zero-sum threat to communal identity.

Second, it leads to a profound distortion of sacred texts through bureaucratic overreach. Authoritarian and populist politics frequently weaponise scriptures to justify state-sanctioned exclusion or the restriction of basic freedoms.
Instead of elevating public morality through social justice, religion is too often co-opted by state machinery as a shallow marketing proxy.

This political co-optation was starkly highlighted by the public outcry over restrictive Selangor state planning guidelines. By attempting to ban non-Muslim places of worship from commercial shop lots – a policy born out of bureaucratised hyper-regulation – the state bureaucracy treated minority faith communities not as equal partners in society, but as administrative zoning headaches.

Finally, behavioural political science confirms that intense political-religious polarisation actively drives people away from religious institutions. When observers and moderate believers see faith used as a cynical business or a hypocritical political instrument, they distance themselves from it. By transforming a universal faith into a partisan weapon, politicians end up fracturing the very communities they claim to protect.
Preserve the integrity of faith

Faith can and should be a powerful personal motivator for ethical leadership and social justice. When it truly informs politics, it elevates the state, strengthens the rule of law and fosters community under shared moral instincts. But when politics co-opts religion, faith is debased, hypocrisy breeds and polarisation thrives.

When religion is used to chase votes, it loses its soul. If we wish to preserve the integrity of faith as a universal compass for justice and peace in Malaysia, we must insulate it from the corrosive arena of partisan politics.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

As research becomes increasingly interdisciplinary, another challenge is emerging: finding the right capability in the first place. Addressing these challenges was a central theme of the 2026 NEMO User Meeting, hosted by MIT.nano Oct. 5–6. The meeting brought together 65 representatives from 25 laboratories and organizations, including facility directors, laboratory managers, technical staff, software developers, industry representatives, and government researchers. Sponsored by the Northeast Microelectronics Coalition (NEMC) hub, the meeting focused on sharing approaches to lab management and building connections among facilities. At the center of the meeting was the NanoFab Equipment Management and Operations (NEMO) system, an open-source platform that provides tools for managing shared research facilities while allowing individual laboratories to adapt the system to their own needs. The meeting highlighted an important characteristic of the NEMO community: The same platform can serve a very diverse set of facilities, and while the scale or the scientific missions of the facilities may differ, their core operational challenges are often remarkably similar.  For Anna Osherov, associate director of Characterization.nano and organizer of the meeting, the collaborative model is one of the most compelling aspects of NEMO. “Open source changes the way we think about technology development,” she says. “We can build on what others have already developed, contribute improvements back to the community, and collectively create a platform that is more capable than what any one facility could develop on its own.” NEMO was originally released as open-source software by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in 2018. Its community edition (NEMO-CE), launched in 2023, allows facilities to develop and share extensions to the platform. At the October meeting, participants from organizations including MIT; Stanford, Columbia, and Princeton universities; the University of Pennsylvania; NIST; NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory; and Atlantis Labs presented tools to address challenges ranging from chemical management and user administration to equipment status, training, and workflow automation. The range of presentations illustrated how differently configured facilities are adapting a common platform to their own needs. Stanford, for example, presented real-time displays for equipment status and reservations, while Columbia shared its experience migrating to NEMO and extending the system for billing and facility workflows. Princeton demonstrated automated process charts for monitoring tool performance, and the University of Pennsylvania presented approaches to chemical management. Overall, the projects demonstrated the premise behind the NEMO community: a solution developed to address a problem at one facility can become a resource for others. “Together we can do way more than any one of us individually can,” said Vladimir Bulović, director of MIT.nano, during his opening remarks. “NEMO is the platform that gave us, finally, a streamlined way to do so.” From individual facilities to a connected research ecosystem As the NEMO community grows, another opportunity emerges. Universities and research organizations operate specialized facilities, each with unique equipment, expertise, and capabilities. But researchers cannot use a capability they are unaware of or cannot easily find. This is particularly important for microelectronics R&D, where progress often depends on moving quickly between specialized capabilities. A researcher may need fabrication at one facility, advanced characterization at another, specialized microscopy somewhere else, and a process or analysis capability available at only a handful of institutions. Finding those capabilities, and knowing where and when they can be accessed, can itself become a bottleneck.Traditionally, networks of facilities have relied on static webpages or databases to describe available resources. But as facilities evolve, this information can quickly become outdated. At the meeting, MIT.nano presented Hydra, a new open-source platform being developed with support from NEMC as a key component of the NEMC Technical Concierge, a program that aims to help researchers identify and access specialized capabilities across a network of facilities. Hydra is designed to connect multiple NEMO installations and draw information directly from the systems that facilities already use, rather than requiring someone to manually update a separate database. The result is a compilation built from the ground truths of actively-used facility management systems. “Hydra does not replace any lab management system,” Osherov explained. “It connects, synchronizes, and keeps data up to date across all connected systems in real time.” In this model, NEMO provides the operational source of information within an individual facility, while Hydra makes that information discoverable across facilities. For a researcher, that could mean finding a specialized capability without first needing to know which laboratory might have the relevant equipment.  “The focus is to make the distributed infrastructure supporting research more discoverable and usable,” Osherov said. Building infrastructure that can change The approach reflects a broader philosophy: Research infrastructure needs to evolve as research itself changes. “We need to build a flexible research space and a community-oriented space so that people feel empowered to go to it, use it, and then redefine it as the years progress, adapting it to the needs of the next generation of researchers,” said Bulović. That flexibility applies to operational systems as well as physical laboratories. New instruments and research methods emerge, user communities change, and facilities develop new requirements. An open-source platform allows individual facilities to respond to those changes while providing a mechanism for improvements to be shared. At MIT.nano alone, NEMO supports more than 1,600 active researchers using more than 200 tools, with approximately 160,000 hours of tool usage each year. For Jorg Scholvin, associate director of Fab.nano, operating at that scale makes the efficiency of everyday processes, and the ability to adapt and change quickly, important. “A small improvement in an administrative workflow can be multiplied across thousands of users and tens of thousands of equipment interactions,” he said. The NEMO wave The sense of community and positive outlook for the future of shared facilities was apparent throughout the two-day meeting. Closing discussions looked ahead to the role of data integration, automation, and artificial intelligence in lab operations. “The community is taking on a life of its own,” said Mathieu Rampant, CEO and co-founder of Atlantis Labs, describing a model in which facility managers can share ideas and solve problems together. “It’s more sustainable,” he added as he talked about having to do less as the NEMO-CE manager because the facilities managers are talking to each other — sharing ideas and solving problems as a network: “the NEMO wave,” Samantha Roberts, director of the City University of New York nanofabrication facility, called it. “Everyone is invested in it and cares about it. It takes a lot of effort to change your lab management system and if we keep this going, we can build out something that’s really cool and that works.” For Osherov, the purpose remains straightforward. “Ultimately, this is about enabling research. The better we can manage the operational side of our facilities, the more effectively we can make our instruments, expertise, and capabilities available to the research community.” In microelectronics, where innovation increasingly depends on access to specialized and distributed capabilities, that availability matters. The ability to find the right capability at the right facility, using information drawn directly from actively used systems, can help researchers move more quickly from an idea to an experiment to real-world application and impact.

How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.

While game theory predicts how rational actors behave under particular rules, reverse game theory designs rules to elicit the behavior we want. Think of splitting a cake: if one person cuts it and the other gets first choice, the cutter has an incentive to make the portions equal.
Researchers believe the approach could align AI more closely with our rules and instructions. But big questions remain about whether these mechanisms will work in practice.
Here’s how reverse game theory could help make AI agents behave.

c064ec7bcbb77124: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).
The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.
The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linus Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links].
The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”
Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”
“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.

“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”

The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.

“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”
Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number
9de50d9e2df39599: Baru-baru ini calon muda Pakatan Harapan (PH) bagi kerusi Kuala Linggi pada PRN Melaka, menarik perhatian ramai apabila mendakwa berjaya membantu menyelesaikan masalah penalti cukai lebih RM70,000 yang menghimpit sebuah persatuan nelayan sejak beberapa tahun lalu. Kemudian calon tersebut mengisytiharkan ‘This is how Gen Z works (beginilah cara Gen Z bekerja)’.

Kenyataan itu mengundang pelbagai reaksi. Penyokong parti menyatakan inilah generasi yang kita mahu, muda dan pantas tidak seperti pemimpin tua yang lambat, malas dan banyak main politik. Penyokong parti lawan pula sudah pastilah mentertawakan dan memperlekehkan kenyataan tersebut. Katanya 'budak ini' berangan.

Dakwaan calon tersebut menggambarkan seolah-olah selama ini orang tua tidak mampu menjadi pelaksana yang berkesan. Memang di media sosial pun sering kita lihat warga Malaysia bawah 60 tahun menyatakan rasa muaknya melihat muka pak cik-pak cik di Parlimen yang telah pun mereka lihat sejak kecil lagi. Sebab itu selalu timbul saranan agar kita tolak pemimpin tua dalam pilihan raya.

Soalannya, apakah sekarang kita benar-benar perlukan orang muda sebagai peneraju barisan hadapan dalam pentadbiran negara? Dan kali ini calon Gen Z sendiri telah mengangkat dirinya dan mendakwa generasinya mampu mengambil alih kerja ini dengan lebih efisien.

Di Threads sering saya lihat Gen Z bertekak dengan Gen Y (milenial). Masing-masing mahu membuktikan generasi merekalah paling bagus. Maksudnya, kami Gen X dan Boomers ni kira dinosaurlah, kena duduk di tepi diam-diam.

Tapi benar, memang perkembangan dunia hari ini sedang menyaksikan kebangkitan politik anak muda. Di Nepal, demonstrasi besar-besaran pada September 2025 yang digerakkan anak muda akibat kemarahan terhadap rasuah, nepotisme dan sekatan media sosial akhirnya membawa kepada kejatuhan kerajaan. Pada Mac 2026, Balendra Shah, bekas penyanyi rap berusia 35 tahun muncul sebagai perdana menteri baharu negara itu. Walaupun Shah sendiri tergolong dalam Gen Y, naiknya dia sebagai perdana menteri tidak dapat dipisahkan daripada gelombang perubahan yang digerakkan oleh Gen Z.

Di Kenya, anak muda bangkit menentang dasar percukaian dan tekanan ekonomi. Di Madagascar, anak muda bangkit melawan kerajaan. Di Maghribi menyaksikan gerakan bernama 'Gen Z 212' mendesak kerajaan melakukan pembaharuan pendidikan dan perkhidmatan kesihatan. Seperti kesan domino, walaupun tiada kaitan di antara mereka, kebangkitan anak muda ini semakin melebar ke serata dunia.

Paling baru bulan lepas dan masih berlaku, anak muda Perancis bangkit memprotes besar-besaran isu pendidikan sehingga memberikan tekanan kepada Presiden Emmanuel Macron. Gelombang rakyat kemudiannya menjadi makin besar dan merebak sehingga menarik penyertaan mahasiswa, kesatuan sekerja dan masyarakat umum memprotes isu-isu lain juga.

Ini memperlihatkan satu fenomena di mana golongan yang selama ini sering dianggap lembik dan cepat layu seperti strawberi tiba-tiba mampu mengucar-ngacirkan kestabilan politik sebuah negara. Apakah Malaysia juga sedang bergerak ke arah itu? Nampaknya calon Kuala Linggi ini cuba membayangkan bahawa proses pengambilalihan anak muda boleh bermula.

Melihat perkembangan dunia, kita tahu protes anak muda di jalan raya bukan perkara baru tetapi perlu ditegaskan bahawa menjatuhkan kerajaan dengan mentadbir kerajaan merupakan dua perkara berbeza. Semua orang boleh marah dan turun memprotes menumbangkan kerajaan. Semua orang boleh berceramah tetapi bukan semua boleh merangka dasar, merancang belanjawan dan mengurus ekonomi. Yang dulu kaki demo, kini sudah jadi menteri pun kita dapat lihat dia masih terpinga-pinga. Yang dah berhenti jadi menteri pun kita lihat banyak bercakap di podcast komplen sana-sini walhal sewaktu jadi menteri entah apa yang dia buat, tak nampak pun hasilnya.

Sebenarnya, kemunculan pemimpin muda bukan perkara baharu dalam sejarah politik negara kita. Najib Razak menjadi Ahli Parlimen ketika berusia 23 tahun, dilantik sebagai timbalan menteri pada usia 25 tahun dan menjadi menteri besar Pahang ketika berusia 29 tahun.

'Pengantin baru' Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman pun pernah menjadi menteri belia dan sukan pada usia 25 tahun. Kini, di kementerian sama menyaksikan Mohammed Taufiq Johari, menjawat jawatan menteri dalam usia tak sampai 30 tahun. Maknanya, kebolehan orang muda memimpin memang sentiasa diiktiraf. Bezanya dulu kita tidak melabelkan seseorang mengikut generasi yang bunyinya macam bunyi model telefon pintar atau kereta. Gen itulah, gen inilah!

Sebenarnya, saya sendiri rimas dengan label dan pembahagian kategori manusia kepada Baby Boomers, Gen X, Gen Y, Gen Z, Alpha dan bermacam-macam generasi lagi. Bagi saya, label tersebut bukanlah ketetapan saintifik yang mutlak. Label generasi yang pada asalnya digunakan dalam kajian sosial ini kemudian telah menjadi alat pemasaran dalam dunia perniagaan.

Dalam dunia pemasaran, pengguna perlu dikenal pasti, dikelompokkan supaya produk dapat dijual dengan lebih berkesan. Meletakkan label pada generasi adalah satu jalan mudah untuk tujuan tersebut. Masalah yang timbul ialah apabila kategori pemasaran ini mula dianggap sebagai kebenaran fakta tentang sifat manusia. Boomers beginilah, Gen X begitulah, kononnya mereka lebih lasak tapi menjadi hamba pekerjaan. Generasi sekarang pula lebih pintarlah, tetapi lembik macam strawberi. Macam saya kata tadi, kebenaran teori itu tidak mutlak dan bergantung kepada banyak faktor.

Padahal, perbezaan yang diperdebatkan selalu ini hanya sekadar pertembungan biasa antara golongan tua dengan orang muda. Orang muda dulu pun memberontak dan mempertikaikan kewibawaan orang tua yang dirasakan sudah mula tumpul. Kita waktu muda dahulu pun rebel, mahu bebas dan bercita-cita mengubah dunia. Manakala orang tua adatnya pula sentiasa meragui keupayaan anak muda. Macam kita hari ini berat untuk menyerahkan baton kerana menganggap anak muda masih belum cukup matang dan kurang pengalaman.

Di Malaysia pula, budaya politiknya memang sudah 'begitu' sejak sekian lama. Anak muda yang mahu menjadi pemimpin kebanyakannya masih perlu melalui struktur parti yang dikuasai generasi tua. Mereka perlu mendapat restu kepimpinan, mematuhi disiplin parti dan menyesuaikan diri dengan budaya politik sedia ada ini. Pendek kata, dengan acuan politik tua, Gen Z yang berada di dalamnya pun akan kelihatan poyo dan tak menarik. Itulah yang berlaku ketika Baby Boomers, Gen X dan milenial masih muda. Mahu mengubah, bercakap lantang tentang kebangkitan anak muda tetapi akhirnya tersedut ke dalam lubang yang sama.

Apakah boleh terjadi satu gelombang di mana anak muda Gen Z beramai-ramai menyertai mana-mana parti politik besar tanah air dan melakukan 'serang hendap' mengambil alih tampuk kepimpinan lama lalu melakukan reformasi politik? Sempatkah mereka naik atau belum apa-apa mereka semua akan dicantas?

Kepada calon Kuala Linggi, saya mengalu-alukan calon muda tetapi saya kira keberkesanan seseorang pemimpin bukan diukur dengan cepat atau lambatnya mendapat tandatangan perdana menteri. Itu masih belum dianggap satu perubahan. Dan kalau itulah yang dikatakan sebagai satu kerja, ia bukanlah sesuatu yang membanggakan. Budaya surat sokongan, budaya potong barisan guna kabel politik bukan perkara baru dan bukan budaya yang sihat.

Jika Gen Z bercita-cita untuk melakukan reformasi, ia harus mempercekapkan sistem pentadbiran itu sendiri tanpa banyak kerenah birokrasi dalam menyelesaikan masalah rakyat. Jika itu berjaya, kita tak perlukan hubungan istimewa wakil rakyat dengan Perdana Menteri untuk meluluskan sebarang pekerjaan. Kita mahu kecekapan sistem itu sendiri yang memainkan peranan dengan berkesan. Itu yang harus anak muda Gen Z ubah jika berjaya menjadi perangka dasar di Dewan Rakyat.

Persoalan sama ada Gen Z mampu memimpin negara tidak boleh dijawab dengan melihat kad pengenalan, kepetahan berpidato, jumlah 'follower' TikTok atau aktif menghasilkan video. Kita memerlukan pemimpin yang memahami tanggungjawab, mempunyai keberanian membuat keputusan, menghormati institusi dan sanggup dipertanggungjawabkan apabila melakukan kesilapan. Ciri-ciri tersebut tetap ada pada sesetengah pemimpin tua kita hari ini. Sekiranya ada ahli politik dari Gen Z yang tidak memenuhi kriteria tersebut, pada saya dia hanyalah mesin baharu dengan program lama.

Sesebuah negara itu hebat kerana pemimpinnya sentiasa mempunyai idea segar, bertenaga dan bersemangat melaksanakan visinya tanpa mengira berapa pun usianya. Tetapi jika pemimpin generasi muda terus membawa perangai politik lama yang poyo dan main -main, nescaya kita tidak akan ke mana-mana. Harap muka sahaja muda, idea dan wawasannya tetap lapuk. Buat apa? Kepada calon muda Kuala Linggi, jika cita-cita anda memang mahukan perubahan, 'pak cik' sokong!

de929831445c05d5: Walaupun seminggu sudah berlalu saya terpanggil menulis mengenai Perjanjian Keyakinan dan Perbekalan dimeterai antara kerajaan, Ahli Parlimen Bersatu, bekas Ahli Parlimen parti itu yang menyokong PMX dan Ahli Parlimen Muar Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman.

Sebab? Perikatan Nasional memutuskan tidak akan ikut sama yakni tidak akan menandatangani perjanjian itu yang ramai lebih gemar guna istilah Inggerisnya iaitu CSA untuk Confidence and Supply Agreement.
Keengganan PN memeterai CSA bukanlah sesuatu yang memeranjatkan walaupun pendapat umum ialah CSA peluang perkukuh kestabilan politik negara.

Dan kestabilan politik adalah antara prasyarat penting untuk memastikan dasar kerajaan dapat dilaksanakan dengan berkesan dan manfaatnya dapat dirasai rakyat, dalam sebuah negara yang sedang berdepan pelbagai cabaran ekonomi dan tuntutan pembangunan. At least that’s how Segamat MP R Yuneswaran look at it.

PN jelas tidak bersependapat lalu tidak menerima CSA. Itu hak mereka. Cuma yang menarik bagi saya ialah rakan baik PN (khususnya dalam menghadapi PRN Melaka) iaitu Pengerusi BN Zahid Hamidi menyarankan CSA diperluas kepada lebih banyak parti sama ada daripada kerajaan atau pembangkang.

Kata Zahid apa yang dilakukan ini (CSA) satu langkah baik dan pernah dilaksanakan kerajaan ketika wakil Umno jadi perdana menteri. Kata-kata ini buat saya tersenyum lebar. Mengapa? Jawapannya di penghujung artikel ini. Lantas pada hemat saya apa yang dikata Zahid amat menarik atas dua sebab.
Sebab pertama kerana saranan Zahid dibuat semasa PN dan BN semakin mesra. Dan apabila PN tolak CSA bererti mereka tolak juga saranan Zahid.
Sebab kedua ialah apabila Zahid berkata (saya ulang ) “apa yang dilakukan ini (CSA) satu langkah baik dan pernah dilaksanakan kerajaan ketika wakil Umno jadi perdana menteri”.

Wakil Ummo jadi perdana menteri yang dimaksudkan kita tahu ialah Ismail Sabri Yaakob. Apa yang berlaku? Tentu ramai masih ingat. Pada September 2021, Ismail memeterai apa yang dipanggil memorandum persefahaman dan kestabilan politik dengan Anwar Ibrahim yang waktu itu ketua pembangkang.
Kata Anwar, memorandum itu menjadi kenyataan kerana sikap positif Ismail yang mengambil pendekatan berunding segera dengan pembangkang sebaik dilantik perdana menteri kesembilan.

Perlu dinyatakan memorandum itu bukan CSA per se. Ini diakui Anwar sendiri waktu itu. Apa pun dalam dokumen MoU antara Pakatan Harapan dengan kerajaan pimpinan Ismail, kerajaan menjanjikan sejumlah reformasi dalam jangka waktu tertentu dan juga berjanji untuk tidak membubarkan Parlimen sebelum 31 Julai 2022.

Sebagai balasan PH pula berjanji tidak akan menggunakan undi mereka menggulingkan Ismail atau menyekat Belanjawan 2022 selagi pembaharuan dijanjikan mengikut jadual dan pembangkang dilibatkan dalam perbincangan Rang Undang-undang Perbekalan. Di samping itu PH berjanji membantu usaha kerajaan memerangi wabak Covid-19 yang melanda waktu itu.

Put simply the MoU was a good thing for the country considering the circumstance then. Namun, Zahid dan Umno menekan Ismail untuk mengadakan pilihan raya umum dengan segera kerana berpendapat Umno sedang berada pada tahap meyakinkan untuk menang. Zahid konon mahu Ismail strike while the iron is still hot.
Tindakan Zahid dan Umno boleh dilihat sebagai tidak memberi ruang kepada Ismail menjayakan MoU beliau dengan PH.

Tekanan demi tekanan dikenakan ke atas Ismail. Menyulitkan Ismail ialah beliau sekadar seorang naib presiden Umno manakala Zahid presiden parti . Akhirnya, Ismail tidak ada pilihan melainkan tunduk akur. Parlimen dibubarkan pada Oktober 2022 dan PRU15 diadakan pada November 2022.
Dan Umno/BN mencatat prestasi paling buruk dalam sejarah mereka. Umno hanya menang 27 kerusi, MCA (2) dan MIC (1). Perkiraan Zahid meleset.

Fast forward CSA yang dimeterai 29 Okt lalu. Pada upacara tandatangan kerajaan diketuai Timbalan Perdana Menteri II Fadillah Yusof. Bukan timbalan perdana menteri I. Kita tahu siapa pemegang jawatan itu.
Mungkinkah ini kerana pendirian lalu Zahid terhadap MoU 2021 dan tindakan susulannya yang boleh dilihat sebagai bertentangan dengan semangat MoU itu?
Maka, kerana itulah saya tersenyum lebar seperti disebut tadi apabila Zahid memuji CSA 2026 dan mahu ia diperluas kepada semua parti.

1a7942fb3b9f842f: Diplomacy is not always measured by grand agreements, historic handshakes or comprehensive peace settlements.
Sometimes, its effectiveness is demonstrated through small but tangible improvements in human lives.
The recent decision by Myanmar’s military authorities to begin releasing ethnic Rakhine deportees following Malaysian diplomatic pressure is one such development.
According to The Irrawaddy, the releases followed Malaysia’s intervention over the detention of individuals deported from Malaysia to Myanmar.
This is hardly a diplomatic breakthrough. Yet it is not insignificant.
It demonstrates that Putrajaya’s decision to maintain engagement with Nay Pyi Taw, despite international criticism, can produce limited but measurable results.
More baby steps are needed.
First, engagement must never be confused with endorsement.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has faced criticism for engaging Myanmar’s military leadership, particularly Senior General now President Min Aung Hlaing.
Critics argue that such engagement risks legitimising a regime responsible for widespread displacement, military violence and the destruction of democratic institutions.
These concerns are valid.

However, refusing to communicate with the authorities exercising power in Nay Pyi Taw would make it harder for Malaysia to secure detainees’ release, negotiate humanitarian access or protect vulnerable returnees.
Diplomacy requires contact, even with governments whose conduct one fundamentally opposes.
The purpose is not to confer legitimacy but to influence behaviour.
Second, the releases demonstrate the potential value of sustained diplomatic pressure.
Malaysia raised concerns about the treatment of its deportees. Foreign minister Mohamad Hasan sought clarification. Myanmar subsequently began releasing those detained.
Although this sequence does not prove that Malaysian pressure alone led to the releases, it suggests that diplomatic intervention mattered.
Malaysia did not merely accept Myanmar’s treatment of the deportees. It demanded accountability.
This is how engagement should function: dialogue accompanied by expectations, verification and humanitarian safeguards.
Third, piecemeal progress must not conceal Myanmar’s larger humanitarian catastrophe.
Without a doubt, Myanmar remains deeply fractured.
The military authorities do not exercise uncontested control over the entire country.
Ethnic armed organisations and resistance forces remain powerful actors.
Rakhine State is particularly complicated because of the continuing conflict involving the Arakan Army and Myanmar’s military.
Repatriation cannot automatically be considered safe merely because some detainees have been released.
Malaysia must distinguish between voluntary returns and deportations that expose vulnerable people to persecution, detention or forced recruitment.
The principle of non-refoulement must remain central.
Fourth, Malaysia needs stronger mechanisms to monitor returnees.
Diplomatic assurances are meaningful only when independently verified.
Malaysia should work with relevant UN agencies and humanitarian organisations to establish procedures for monitoring the welfare of those returned.
Such arrangements should protect family contact, freedom from arbitrary detention and access to humanitarian assistance.
Without verification, Malaysia risks celebrating releases without knowing whether those individuals subsequently enjoy meaningful security.
Fifth, Asean must translate Malaysia’s incremental progress into collective diplomatic action.
To be sure, the Asean Five-Point Consensus has struggled to end Myanmar’s conflict.
Nevertheless, its fundamental objectives remain relevant: reducing violence, encouraging inclusive dialogue and facilitating humanitarian assistance.
Malaysia’s bilateral engagement should complement these objectives, not replace them.
The Philippines, as Asean Chair in 2026, should consider how such diplomatic openings can strengthen regional cooperation.
Asean needs more than repeated expressions of concern.
It needs Asean’s resolve to translate principles into practical humanitarian outcomes.
Sixth, engagement must extend beyond Myanmar’s military leadership.
Malaysia should maintain communication with the National Unity Government (the Myanmar government-in-exile), ethnic armed organisations, civil society and humanitarian networks.
Myanmar’s fragmentation makes broader engagement indispensable.
A settlement negotiated exclusively with military authorities cannot guarantee acceptance throughout the country.
Malaysia must broaden and deepen its diplomatic channels without abandoning humanitarian principles.
Finally, Anwar’s approach should be judged by outcomes rather than appearances.
Malaysia cannot single-handedly resolve Myanmar’s civil war.
But neither should it abandon opportunities to secure modest improvements in human security.
The release of Rakhine deportees is encouraging, although it does not establish that Myanmar has fundamentally changed.
Further progress requires humanitarian access, independent monitoring, safeguards for returnees and eventually inclusive political dialogue.
Myanmar’s crisis cannot be resolved overnight. Yet diplomatic paralysis is not a strategy.
Malaysia must remain principled without becoming immobilised by the complexity of Myanmar’s conflict.
The journey towards peace may begin with small humanitarian concessions rather than spectacular diplomatic breakthroughs.
More baby steps are needed. But genuine, verifiable and sustainable piecemeal progress is still progress.
For Myanmar’s long-suffering people, even modest improvements in human security matter.
